newsitem.title: HUNGARY: TELLER TELLS HUNGARY TO TRUST NUCLEAR ENERGY.
newsitem.headline: TELLER TELLS HUNGARY TO TRUST NUCLEAR ENERGY.

text.p: Edward Teller, the Hungarian born physicist often dubbed the father of the America's hydrogen bomb, on Monday encouraged Hungary to further develop its Soviet-designed nuclear energy programme.

"Nuclear energy is how Hungary can make a lot of real progress for all people to live better," Teller told Reuters during a visit to the country's nuclear energy plant at Paks on the Danube, which generates 40 percent of the country's energy needs.

Teller, who is on a two-week visit to Hungary at the invitation of Prime Minister Gyula Horn, was a key member of the team which designed and built the the first atomic weapon, dropped by the United States on Japan in 1945.
Teller said Hungary should not worry about its relatively large depenedence on nuclear power.
"They are doing it in a very expert way and therefore it is right," he said.
The frail, 88-year-old Teller, who emigrated from Hungary to the United States before World War Two, said he was impressed by the Soviet technology and Hungary's safety standards.
"This plant looks to be very well thought out and very safe," he told Reuters.

The four-block pressurised water reactor at Paks was the first former eastern bloc facility to benefit from International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and European Union funding to upgrade its safety systems and is now considered one of the safest Soviet-designed reactors.

The WWER pressurised water reactor type is different from the reactor which melted down at Chernobyl in the Ukraine in 1986 in a disaster which Teller said has still only resulted in 100 deaths and not the tens of thousands people predicted.

"This is the second generation of these reactors," Teller told reporters. "It works well because the people here know what they're doing. It was a good Soviet design with Finnish and Hungarian engineers involved," he said.

However, Teller had some words of warning for the Hungarian government over its plans to invite tenders for foreign companies to take stakes in the Paks plant in the second phase of an energy privatisation programme which last year saw Western comanies invest over $2 billon in the sector.
"I like privatisation, but in the case of atomic energy only if the state is finally responsible for the work and security." he said.
After his tour, Teller was shown a newly completed bronze bust of his likeness which stands outside the main gate of the Moscow-sponsored plant.

Also represented in a tribute ironically dedicated to the Hungarian contribution to the United States' atomic weapons programme of World War II are the two other Hungarians involved in the project physicists Leo Szilard and Nobel prize winner Eugene Wigner. @
"I'm only sorry they used such a poor model," said Teller of his own statue. (Shiels reachable on +3630 485561)
